newsitem.title: USA: USSR pierced France, Britain early -U.S. documents.
newsitem.headline: USSR pierced France, Britain early -U.S. documents.

text.p: The ultra-secretive U.S. National Security Agency lifted the veil on Tuesday on decoded Second World War messages showing stunning, early Soviet spy successes against Britain and France.

The so-called "Venona" documents, the fifth set made public under an openness initiative begun last year, also shed new light on Soviet spies inside the U.S. wartime programme to develop the atomic bomb.

For example a newly released Soviet intelligence message suggests an earlier than previously known recruitment of Klaus Fuchs, the German-born physicist who was part of the British team in Los Alamos, New Mexico, where the bomb was developed.

The message, dated August 10, 1941, refers to the GRU, the Red Army's intelligence directorate, re-establishing contact in Britain with Fuchs and learning from him "about early efforts to develop the atomic bomb." The National Security Agency provided an overview of the material on its World Wide Web site (www.nsa.gov:8080).
The newly released documents include material that helped unmask star Soviet agents Kim Philby, Guy Burgess and Donald McLean, all ranking British officials.

Another apparent early Soviet success was the reported penetratation of Charles de Gaulle's London-based Free French exile government. A cable from intelligence officers in London to their bosses in Moscow about GRU agents in de Gaulle's movement was dated July 17, 1940, only months after he fled to Britain to escape the German occupation of France.

The decoded cables contain extensive intelligence reporting on Hitler's 1940 "Battle of Britain" air assault, the expected German invasion, preparations of British forces and emergency procedures of the GRU, including setting up at least three clandestine radio stations.

They also disclose the existence of an unidentified agent codenamed "Baron," who apparently reported secrets gleaned from British cracking of the Nazis' Enigma codes, which gave the allies a window on German battle plans.

At the time, the Soviet Union was allied with Britain, France, the United States and other allied powers against Germany, Italy and Japan. Venona was the final NSA codeword for the successful joint U.S.-British cracking of 1940s Soviet cable traffic.

In its overview of the newly released material, the National Security Agency said the head of the GRU operation in London "probably" was Simon Kremer, "who had the cover assignment of private secretary to the military attache."
The NSA did not say whether Kremer was still alive. It withheld the names of some people referenced in the documents to protect their privacy.

John Haynes, a Library of Congress historian who is a co-author of the 1995 book "The Secret World of American Communism," said the Venona material as a whole documented a sweeping Soviet penetration of the West.
"It is no shock, I suppose, that the Soviets had intelligence operations in various places, but the sheer size of it, all over the place, impresses me," he said in an interview.
